exam_points: Medicine: same human questions, changing explanations and methods.
Three frameworks: balance and harmony, faith and divine will, evidence and technology (they coexisted).
Four kinds of progress: scientific, therapeutic, ethical, social.
Anatomy = Greek anatome, dissection; interest rose and fell in waves.
Egypt: embalming, practical not scientific. Greece: surface anatomy, little human dissection.
Galen: gladiators, animal dissection, teleology; his errors lasted centuries.
Vesalius, De humani corporis fabrica, 1543. Leonardo: Vitruvian Man.
Percussion: Auenbrugger 1761. Auscultation: Laennec.
Burke and Hare → British Anatomy Act 1832. Gray's Anatomy 1858 (Carter's drawings).
Physiology = physis + logos. Debates: vitalism/mechanism, teleology/empiricism, speculation/experiment.
Humours: blood-air-warm, phlegm-water-cold, yellow bile-fire-dry, black bile-earth-cold.
Galen's spirits: natural-liver, vital-heart, animal-brain; blood made in the liver, septal pores.
Pulmonary circulation: Ibn al-Nafis (13th c.), Servetus (1553, burned in Geneva).
Harvey: circulation, heart as pump. Descartes: dualism, pineal gland.
Mayow: part of air for combustion and life. Galvani: frog muscle, animal electricity.
Comte: theological, metaphysical, positive stages. Bell-Magendie law. Magendie's journal 1821.
Claude Bernard: experimental method, milieu intérieur. Beaumont and St Martin: digestion is chemical.
First Nobel 1901 (von Behring). Nuremberg Code 1947, Helsinki 1964, PETA 1980.
Broca 1861 (left frontal lobe, speech). Penfield: cortical maps.

high_yield.html: Anatomy timeline: Egypt (embalming) → Greece (surface anatomy, little dissection) → Galen (animal dissection, teleology) → Middle Ages (Galen rules) → Vesalius 1543 → Auenbrugger 1761 (percussion), Laennec (auscultation) → Anatomy Act 1832 → Gray's 1858.
Galen's spirits, from the bottom up: L-H-B: Liver = Natural, Heart = Vital, Brain = Animal.
Humours: blood-air-warm, phlegm-water-cold, yellow bile-fire-dry, black bile-earth-cold. Lasted 2,000+ years.
Pulmonary circulation before Harvey: Ibn al-Nafis (13th century) and Servetus (1553, burned in Geneva for his religious views). Galen's version: pores in the septum.
Harvey: circulation, heart = pump, quantitative argument. Descartes: dualism (res cogitans / res extensa), pineal gland, heart moved by heat.
19th century: Bell-Magendie (sensory vs motor roots), Magendie's journal 1821, Claude Bernard (milieu intérieur), Beaumont + St Martin (digestion is chemical, 1822).
Ethics: Nazi experiments → Nuremberg Code 1947 (voluntary consent); Helsinki 1964; PETA 1980. Burke and Hare → regulated dissection.
Firsts: first Nobel in Physiology or Medicine 1901, von Behring (diphtheria serum). Broca 1861: left frontal lobe, speech. Penfield: cortical maps.

deeper.title: Why Galen lasted so long
deeper.html:
Galen's system explained nutrition, life and movement in one coherent scheme, his writings were copied and taught for centuries, and his idea of life-sustaining spirits fitted religious ideas of the soul. Human dissection was rare, so few people could check him. That is why the booklet uses him to show how a source's reputation can become stronger than the evidence, and why Harvey's quantitative argument mattered so much: it replaced authority with a test anyone could repeat.

Source: the booklet's chapters on anatomy and physiology; Ribatti, William Harvey and the discovery of the circulation of the blood.

deeper.title: From milieu intérieur to homeostasis
deeper.html:
Claude Bernard noticed that living organisms keep their internal conditions steady even when the outside world changes. He called the fluid that bathes the cells the milieu intérieur. Later physiologists turned this idea into homeostasis: the active regulation of temperature, glucose and body-fluid composition that you study in physiology today.

Source: the booklet; Wikipedia, Internal environment.

exam_points: Stages of social reaction: denial → panic/flight → explanations → control measures → new normal.
Black Death 1348 killed ~30% of Europe; Yersinia pestis, black rat, flea; quarantine invented.
Syphilis: 'French disease', 1490s, Treponema pallidum, penicillin.
Leprosy: Mycobacterium leprae, Hansen's disease, extreme stigma for a mildly contagious disease.
Cholera: John Snow linked it to drinking water in 1854; Vibrio cholerae identified 1884.
Smallpox: Jenner 1798 (cowpox protects against smallpox); eradicated 9 December 1979.
Tuberculosis: leading adult killer of the 19th century; sanatoria; McKeown 1970.
1918 influenza: 25–100 million deaths.
AIDS: USA 1981, initially 'GRID'.
Moroccan oil tragedy 1959: paralysis epidemic, Meknes.

deeper.title: Why quarantine means forty days
deeper.html:
Venice and Ragusa held incoming ships for 'quaranta giorni', forty days, before crews could land, because plague seemed to burn itself out in that time. The number was guessed, but it exceeded the incubation period and the disease course, so it worked. The lecture's point stands: an effective control measure was found long before the cause was known.

Source: the lecture's plague control measures slide.

deeper.title: Why the 1918 flu killed young adults
deeper.html:
Most influenza kills the very old and very young, but the 1918 strain killed healthy 20-to-40-year-olds. The leading explanation is an overwhelming immune response — a 'cytokine storm' — in the strongest immune systems, plus crowding of soldiers in the last year of the war. It is why the pandemic reshaped epidemic-control institutions, as the lecture notes.

Source: the lecture's influenza slide.

provenance.note: Medical Art handout.pdf (History of Medicine & Medical Art, Pr Maryam Fourtassi)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Contempt = one raised eyebrow, sideways glance, curled lip; a mix of anger and disgust.
Disgust = wrinkled nose bridge, curled upper lip. Surprise = wide eyes, arched brows, open mouth.
Five keys of emotional intelligence: self-awareness, self-regulation, empathy, social skills, motivation.
Social styles: pragmatic/performance-driven vs humanistic/relationship-driven.
Self-regulation = thoughtful acting over reacting; short-term (breathing, grounding) and long-term tools (journaling, self-compassion).
Empathy has cognitive (perspective-taking), emotional (feeling) and behavioural (compassion) dimensions.
Disagree with grace: understand feelings rather than convince.
Thomas-Kilmann conflict model: own interests vs cooperation.
Non-violent communication: observation → feeling → need → request.

deeper.title: Why naming a feeling calms it
deeper.html:
The empathic replies in the lecture all start by naming the emotion — embarrassed, overwhelmed, discouraged — before offering anything. Putting a feeling into words engages the reflective parts of the brain and dampens the alarm response, which is why the person feels calmer and heard even before any problem is solved. Advice given before that step usually lands as judgement.

Source: the lecture's empathy scenarios.

deeper.title: Why 'but' undoes empathy
deeper.html:
'I understand how you feel, but...' tells the listener that the first half was a formality. The lecture's three examples all follow this shape and all end by declaring the other person wrong. Non-violent communication avoids the trap by separating observation, feeling and need from the request, so disagreement can be expressed without cancelling the acknowledgement.

Source: the lecture's empathy and NVC slides.

exam_points: Five functions of pathology: explain, identify (diagnosis), predict (prognosis), justify treatment, prove/refute (autopsy, forensic).
Illness = patient's suffering (constant); disease = medical idea (changing).
Physiological theories: what the patient is; ontological theories: what the patient has.
Hippocrates on the Sacred Disease (epilepsy): natural cause, phlegm in the brain.
Rhazes distinguished fevers with and without rash (9th c.); Sydenham described gout and dropsy.
Morgagni 1761: The Seats and Causes of Diseases — birth of anatomical pathology.
Microscope in the 1830s; Virchow described leukaemia in 1846 and brought cell theory to pathology.
Pasteur (bacteria–disease), Lister (carbolic acid antisepsis), Koch (M. tuberculosis, Nobel 1905).
Germ theory triumphed in the 1880s; vaccines (Joseph Meister).
DNA discovered 1952 by Watson and Crick (Nobel 1962).
Phrenology (Franz Gall) — a refuted theory once accepted.

deeper.title: Why 'illness' and 'disease' are different words
deeper.html:
The lecture separates the patient's experience (illness: fever, pain, fear, unchanged across centuries) from the doctor's explanation (disease: humours, then lesions, then germs, then genes). Keeping them apart explains why a patient can feel very ill with no disease found, or carry a disease without feeling ill — the situation the microscope created in the 1830s.

Source: the lecture's illness and disease slide.

deeper.title: Why phrenology is the cautionary tale
deeper.html:
Franz Gall reasoned that brain regions with distinct functions would enlarge and push the skull outward, so character could be read from bumps. The premise of localisation was partly right, the method was wrong, and the theory was still accepted by respectable science for decades. It shows the lecture's warning: each era's pathology is validated by that era's science, and today's certainties deserve the same scrutiny.

Source: the lecture's case of phrenology slide.

exam_points: Pharmakon = drug, remedy and poison.
Similia similibus curantur (like cures like, homeopathy) vs contraria contrariis curantur (opposite cures opposite).
Mithridate (1st c. BC) and Theriac: poison antidotes with a mystical aura until the 19th century.
Galen: galenical pharmacology, healing power of nature, about 300 medications.
15th century: metals (copper, sulphur, salt, mercury); mercury for syphilis, antimony for everything.
Apothecaries: ancient pharmacists, mostly women; botany taught until the 20th century.
Fleming: penicillin, widely used by 1945.
Insulin: Banting, Best, Macleod, Collip, Toronto 1922; Nobel 1923; patent sold for one dollar.
James Lind 1747: scurvy trial. Controls 1900s, committees 1930s, randomisation 1940s, blinding after 1940, Nuremberg 1947.
Thalidomide: ~10,000 children in 25 countries; Frances Oldham Kelsey, 1962.

deeper.title: Why theriac survived 1,800 years
deeper.html:
Theriac contained dozens of ingredients, including opium, so it relieved pain and anxiety whatever the disease. Any recovery was credited to the remedy, any failure to the wrong recipe, and the elaborate preparation gave it prestige. It is the lecture's example of a remedy persisting while its explanation changes — and of the placebo effect at work before the word existed.

Source: the lecture's mithridate/theriac and Galen slides.

deeper.title: Why randomisation was the decisive step
deeper.html:
Controls alone can be biased: doctors tend to give the new drug to the patients they think will do well. Randomisation, introduced in the 1940s, removes that choice, and blinding removes the placebo effect on both sides. Together they turn Lind's 1747 comparison into the evidence-based trial the lecture describes.

Source: the lecture's clinical trials slides.

labels: Mysticism and magic; like cures like

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Vitalism vs mechanism; teleology vs empiricism; speculation vs experimentation.
Galen: three spirits (natural/liver, vital/lungs, animal/brain), blood flows outward, pores in the heart.
Ibn al-Nafis described pulmonary circulation in the 13th century; Servetus burned in 1553.
William Harvey (17th c.): the heart is a pump, blood circulates — birth of experimental physiology.
Descartes: mind-body dualism, iatromechanism, soul in the pineal gland.
Mayow: life as combustion (candle and mouse). Galvani: animal electricity.
Bell-Magendie law: motor and sensory nerves. Legallois: respiratory centre in the medulla.
Magendie: Journal de physiologie (1821). Claude Bernard: milieu intérieur, doubt as principle.
Beaumont studied digestion through St. Martin's gastric fistula.
First Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine: 1901.
Nuremberg Code 1947 (10 principles, informed consent first); Declaration of Helsinki 1968.

deeper.title: Why Galen's errors lasted 1,400 years
deeper.html:
Galen dissected animals, not humans, and filled the gaps with a system so complete and purposeful that every observation could be fitted into it. Because the church read the life force as the soul, questioning Galen meant questioning theology. Only when Vesalius dissected humans and Harvey measured blood volume did the facts outrun the system — the lecture's point that mechanism arrived with measurement.

Source: the lecture's antiquity and medieval slides.

deeper.title: Why Claude Bernard's doubt matters
deeper.html:
Bernard's method — observe, localise, alter surgically, watch the effect — only works if the experimenter is willing to be wrong. His 'philosophic doubt' is the opposite of Galenic certainty: a result counts only if it survives the attempt to disprove it. The same doubt underlies the controls and randomisation described in the pharmacology lecture.

Source: the lecture's opening quotation and Claude Bernard slide.

exam_points: Surgery = 'work' + 'hand' (Greek); oldest medical activity, born from warfare.
Trephination 10,000 BC; Tafoughalt (Morocco) mandibular surgery 12,000 BC; splints 2400 BC.
Babylonian code: surgeon's hands cut off for harming a free man.
Edwin Smith Papyrus 1600 BC: 48 case reports; interpreted 1930.
Al-Zahrawi (Abulcasis) dominated medieval surgery.
Ambroise Paré, father of surgery: 'I bandage them but God heals them'.
Royal College of Physicians 1518; Royal College of Surgeons 1843.
Ether 1840s, chloroform 1845; Semmelweis 1847, Lister 1867, rubber gloves 1878.
McBurney appendicitis 1889; Kocher Nobel 1909; Lillehei open heart 1952; Murray kidney transplant 1954 (Nobel 1990); Barnard heart transplant 1967.

deeper.title: Why Semmelweis was ignored
deeper.html:
Semmelweis showed in 1847 that hand-washing with chlorinated lime cut maternal deaths dramatically, but he could not explain why: germ theory was still forty years away. Doctors were offended at being called carriers of death, and a result without a mechanism was easy to dismiss. Lister succeeded twenty years later partly because Pasteur had by then supplied the explanation.

Source: the lecture's antisepsis/asepsis slide.

deeper.title: Why the surgical century began in 1870
deeper.html:
Anaesthesia removed pain in the 1840s and antisepsis removed infection in the 1870s. Only with both could surgeons open the abdomen, chest and skull deliberately rather than as a last resort. The list of firsts in the lecture — gall bladder, appendix, thyroid, heart, transplants — follows directly from those two solved problems.

Source: the lecture's surgical optimism slide.

exam_points: Laennec invented the stethoscope in 1816 by rolling a notebook, for decorum; died of TB at 45.
Van Leeuwenhoek 1670: microscope. Ramón y Cajal: synapses and neuron theory, Nobel 1906.
Electron microscope 1931 (Ruska, Nobel 1986).
Photography 1820s: teaching pathology, chronophotography for movement.
Röntgen: X-rays 1895, Nobel 1901.
Asilomar conference 1975: responsible use of recombinant DNA.
Technology changed the concept of disease (e.g. hypertension) and raises the question of normality.

deeper.title: Why hypertension is a 'technological' disease
deeper.html:
Nobody feels high blood pressure. It became a disease only when the sphygmomanometer made it measurable, and its threshold has been redrawn several times as trials showed benefit from treating lower numbers. The lecture uses it to show that instruments do not just detect disease; they define it, which is why it asks what normality means.

Source: the lecture's consequences of technological developments slide.

deeper.title: Why Laennec's cylinder changed the doctor-patient relationship
deeper.html:
Before 1816 the doctor listened to the patient's story; after it he listened to the chest, and the sound could contradict the story. Physical diagnosis gained authority, the patient's account lost some, and the lecture's 'before and after the stethoscope' marks the shift toward findings over feelings that the history of pathology also describes.

Source: the lecture's Laennec slides.
